# crq Agent Guide

crq is the repo's CLI for autonomous CodeRabbit/Codex pull-request review loops.

Core rule: never post `@coderabbitai review` directly. To drive a PR, call `crq next` and do exactly
what its `.action` says (see Agent Loop below); everything else is reference material.

Every GitHub API operation from an ordinary crq command goes through the persistent `crq serve`
control plane. It owns the shared ETag cache, retries, and rate-limit backoff. GitHub-backed commands
fail closed if it is down. `crq --direct` is an operator recovery tool; agents and daemons must never
use it.

Do not bypass crq to read review status, either. Never hand-poll the GitHub API
(`gh api .../pulls/N/reviews|comments`, looping on the head) to wait for a review
or its outcome: it drains the shared account-wide GitHub REST quota (also spent by
the `crq autoreview` daemon and every other agent, so it exhausts fast) and
competes with crq's own polling. To learn a review's result use `crq loop` (waits
and returns findings) or `crq feedback` (current findings, no trigger); for
queue/quota use `crq status`.

Readiness check:

```bash
crq doctor
```

`crq doctor` emits JSON for agents: crq config, control-plane health, local `gh`, optional CodeRabbit
CLI, and `CODERABBIT_API_KEY` presence.

## Setup

The user must configure `~/.config/crq/env` once:

```bash
export CRQ_REPO=OWNER/crq-state
export CRQ_ISSUE=1
export CRQ_CAL_PR=1
export CRQ_SCOPE=OWNER
export CRQ_STATE_REF=crq-state-v3
# Defaults to the local server. Set these on every client for a shared host:
# export CRQ_SERVER_URL=https://crq.example.test
# export CRQ_SERVER_TOKEN=shared-secret
```

Shared/non-loopback `CRQ_SERVER_URL` values must use HTTPS through a reverse proxy. Plain HTTP is
accepted only for localhost and loopback IP addresses.

`crq serve` must be running, and CodeRabbit native auto-review must be off.

## Agent Loop

**Call `crq next`, do exactly what `.action` says, call it again.** That is the entire loop. Every
judgement an agent used to make — how long to wait, whether the head may move, whether the round is
finished — is a value crq computes.

```bash
crq next OWNER/REPO PR_NUMBER
crq next                      # inside the checkout, the target is inferred
                              # (same for feedback/loop/cancel: omit <repo> <pr>)
```

| `.action` | what to do |
|---|---|
| `fix` | Fix `.findings[]`, validate locally, then `crq resolve` each addressed `.thread_id` (or `crq decline` with a reason). A finding with no `.thread_id` clears with `crq dismiss` once judged — except `source: "review_comment"`, which lost its thread ID to a GraphQL fallback and has to wait for crq to read threads again. Call again. |
| `hold` | Do NOT commit or push: a required reviewer has not answered for this head, and moving the head restarts its review (resolving threads does not). Call again at `.recheck_after`. |
| `push` | The head is released. Commit and push the accumulated fixes once. Call again. |
| `wait` | Nothing to do until `.recheck_after`. |
| `done` | Converged. |
| `blocked` | Needs a human; `.reason` says why (e.g. the PR was closed). |

`crq next` always exits 0 on success — read `.action`, never the exit code. It is non-blocking and
idempotent, and it advances the queue by one step as a side effect, so a PR in a repo outside the
autoreview fleet still progresses. There is no per-PR process to keep alive: if the harness kills
the agent mid-loop, the next `crq next` returns the correct action from persisted state.

Before reading feedback, interactive `next`, `wait`, and `loop` calls take a two-hour renewable work
claim on the PR. Autofix checks the same state in the CAS that grants a fix session, so it cannot
duplicate work the interactive caller has already taken. `done` and `blocked` release it. If you
abandon the loop sooner, run `crq unclaim [OWNER/REPO PR_NUMBER]`; otherwise it expires on its own.

## Waiting

On `wait` or `hold` there is nothing to do yet. Do not sleep, poll, or guess a delay — hand the
wait over and end your turn:

```bash
crq wait OWNER/REPO PR_NUMBER
```

It blocks until there IS something to do (`fix`, `push`, `done`, `blocked`), then prints that same
JSON and exits 0. Run it as your harness's background task: its **exit is the wake event**, so you
burn no tokens idling.

It owns no review round. It renews only the interactive work claim described above, so being killed
cannot wedge review state; the claim expires after two hours. Run it again or call `crq next` to
renew and continue. While idle it watches the shared state ref through `crq serve`; the server's
conditional request receives 304 Not Modified without spending primary REST quota, and the cache is
shared with every other caller. If no review round or live autoreview leader is progressing the PR, `wait`
advances the queue itself and may request a review rather than wait forever.

`crq next --wait` is the same thing inline, for a human at a terminal.

Two rules this replaces, which agents previously had to remember:

- **Never invent a delay.** `.recheck_after` is computed from the account-quota window, the round's
  retry cooldown and the poll interval, and is always at least one poll interval away. Do not
  substitute a timer, guessed review latency, or a `crq status` polling loop.
- **Never decide to push yourself.** `hold` vs `push` is crq's answer. It already accounts for the
  rate-limit degrade (a Codex-only round while CodeRabbit is blocked releases the head, because the
  queued CodeRabbit review fires against whatever head exists when the window opens).

`.local_work` is what separates `push` from `done`: crq checks whether the working copy holds changes
the PR head lacks. Run `crq next` inside the repository checkout so that answer is accurate;
`.local_work_reason` says when it could not be determined.

`crq next --wait` blocks through the states you cannot act on and returns the first actionable
instruction. It shares one code path with the non-blocking form.

### crq loop (interactive/one-shot)

`crq loop` is the older primitive: it triggers a round, blocks until feedback lands, and returns one
report. It remains supported for humans and one-shot scripts, but an agent driving a PR should use
`crq next` — `loop` requires the caller to interpret exit codes and to enforce the hold-the-head and
fix-first rules by hand.

```bash
crq loop OWNER/REPO PR_NUMBER > crq-feedback.json
rc=$?
```

`crq loop` enforces the fix-first invariant for new rounds: unresolved findings are returned before
the PR is queued or a review slot is consumed. Thread-less review-body findings from a previous
commit do not block after fixes are pushed; the next current-head review supersedes them or reports
the finding again.

`crq loop` queues the PR and triggers CodeRabbit when the account can spend a review. Alongside it
crq runs its **co-reviewers** — Codex, Cursor Bugbot and Macroscope (`CRQ_COBOTS`, all enabled by
default). None of them spends CodeRabbit quota or takes the fire slot. Each has a trigger mode
(`CRQ_COBOT_<NAME>_TRIGGER`): `always` posts its command in the same fire step, `selfheal` (the
Bugbot/Macroscope default) only nudges a bot that reviews on its own but missed the head past
`CRQ_COBOT_<NAME>_GRACE`, and `never` posts nothing. crq never triggers a bot that auto-reviews, has
already reviewed the head, or has a check run in flight. A co-reviewer that joins a round uninvited
gates that round's convergence dynamically (an exhaustion notice such as Codex's usage limit, or a
check run reporting the bot cannot review the commit, releases the dynamic gate); one listed in
`CRQ_REQUIRED_BOTS` always gates.

Bugbot and Macroscope report through **check runs** as well as comments — a clean Bugbot round posts
nothing at all on the timeline, so its `Cursor Bugbot` check IS the evidence crq converges on.
`.co_reviewers[<bot>]` reports each one's `reviewed` / `check_state`
(`clean|issues|in_progress|failed|unable|unknown` — `failed` is a crashed run crq re-triggers,
`unable` a bot that reported it cannot review this commit at all, which crq stops waiting for and
never re-triggers) / `verdict`. Macroscope's approvability `verdict`
(`approved|needs_human_review`) is informational only: it never gates convergence and never changes
an exit code. If a bot reports
actionable findings first, it emits them immediately while leaving the queued round alive. Fix and
validate locally and resolve or decline each addressed thread immediately. While any required bot's
`.reviewed_by` value is false, do not commit or push — unless `.coderabbit_deferred` is true and all
non-CodeRabbit required reviewers are true, in which case push freely: the round is Codex-only while
CodeRabbit is rate-limited. Only after every
`CRQ_REQUIRED_BOTS` entry is true for the current head should you fix and resolve the rest, then
commit and push the combined fixes once. Convergence is reported only after that same condition is met.

Exit codes (`crq loop` only — `crq next` always exits 0 and answers in `.action`):
- `0`: done; converged or no actionable findings. Check `.coderabbit_deferred`: when true (with
  `.status == "deferred"`), Codex reviewed clean but the CodeRabbit review is still owed — this is
  progress, NOT convergence (`.converged` stays false). Re-run `crq loop` after
  `.coderabbit_deferred_until` or on the next push; the queued CodeRabbit review fires by itself
  once the window opens.
- `10`: read `.findings[]`, fix valid issues, and validate locally. If any `.reviewed_by` value is
  false, resolve addressed threads but hold the head — EXCEPT when `.coderabbit_deferred` is true
  and all non-CodeRabbit required reviewers are true: those are Codex-only findings during a
  CodeRabbit rate-limit window, so fix, push, and loop again (each Codex round takes minutes;
  several fit inside one CodeRabbit window).
- `2`: timed out waiting for feedback; do not push a stale-feedback round. A HELD pull request is
  not this — it exits `0` with `.status: "held"`, because a hold waits for somebody to lift it or
  for GitHub to report the pull request as merged. Retrying on `2` would spin for ever.

Rate-limit degrade: when CodeRabbit is rate-limited ("Review limit reached … Next review available
in: NN minutes") and Codex demonstrably reviews the PR, the loop degrades to Codex-only rounds
instead of waiting the window out, and the pump posts the co-reviewer triggers for blocked rounds
while keeping the CodeRabbit review queued. Disable with `CRQ_RL_CO_DEGRADE=0` (default on).

`.primary_review_unavailable` (with `.primary_review_unavailable_reason`) means the configured
reviewer will NOT review this head at all — its plan only summarizes, or it skipped the head. When
true: do not hold the head for it, do not wait for it, and IGNORE the account-quota window entirely
(`crq status` may show the account blocked; that block is fleet state and cannot apply to a round
that never spends quota). The round is resolved by the co-reviewers alone, so treat
`.reviewed_by` for the primary as already delivered and act on `.findings` immediately.

Skipped reviews: CodeRabbit may refuse a head outright (`Review skipped` — too many files, no usage
credits). That notice embeds the rate-limit marker but is NOT a timed block: nothing clears by
waiting. crq treats it as "no primary review is coming for this head", converges on the co-reviewers,
never records an account block, and returns the skip as a `major` `source: "review_skipped"` finding
telling you to narrow the PR — the one finding with no thread to resolve, since only changing the PR
addresses it. It binds to the SHA it names, so a split PR is reviewed normally.

Summary-only plans: on a private repo under a Free CodeRabbit plan the bot posts a walkthrough and
never a line-by-line review ("Summarized by CodeRabbit Free … upgrade … for a comprehensive
line-by-line review"). crq reads that notice and runs the co-reviewers alone there — no
`@coderabbitai review` is posted, no fire slot or account quota is spent, and the round converges on
the enabled co-reviewers' evidence instead of hanging on a review that cannot
arrive. Public repos get Pro-grade reviews for free and are unaffected. Nothing to configure: upgrade the plan and crq resumes firing CodeRabbit on
the next observation.

Resolve addressed threads on GitHub (crq keys off GitHub resolution state; a finding keeps
reappearing until its thread is resolved there):

```bash
crq resolve THREAD_ID [THREAD_ID...]
```

After a push, threads from the previous head become outdated and drop out of `findings`, so their
IDs are no longer available there. List every unresolved thread, outdated included:

```bash
crq threads REPO PR
```

Decline a finding you are not addressing. This posts the reason AND resolves the thread — crq reads
GitHub resolution state, so one left open keeps returning `fix`. A contested bot reply is
re-surfaced as its own finding, so nothing is buried. Use `--keep-open` to leave it open on purpose:

```bash
crq decline THREAD_ID [THREAD_ID...] --reason "why declined"
```

If the bot replies contesting a decline you resolved ("I'm retaining the finding: ..."), crq
re-surfaces that reply as a `source: "review_reply"` finding on the next `feedback`/`loop`, so a
convergence never hides a rebuttal you have not answered. Address it or decline again with a stronger
reason; the loop clears it once the bot withdraws (or you stop declining and fix it). Ambiguous bot
replies surface too — crq errs toward showing a possible rebuttal rather than burying it.

Run the whole thing unattended — crq watches every open PR and starts a fix session for the ones
that need one:

```bash
crq autofix install            # prompt + wrapper + service, started; --dry-run to preview
```

Session output goes to `$CRQ_WORKSPACE/logs/<owner>/<name>/<pr>-<head>-<time>.log`. Three consecutive
failures to start a session put `dispatch failing` on the dashboard and status line. That host-health
threshold is independent of `CRQ_DISPATCH_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, which bounds started fix sessions per head.

The service does not inherit your shell. The unit names the config file the install read
(`CRQ_CONFIG`, or `~/.config/crq/env`) and the queue's identity, and the credential has to be one
the service can resolve itself — `gh auth login`, or `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` in that file. A token
exported only in a shell profile makes the install refuse rather than start a watcher that cannot
authenticate.

`crq autofix install` runs `crq watch`, which you can also run yourself:

```bash
crq watch [--no-dispatch] [--once] [--interval 2m] [--concurrency 0] [<repo>...] [-- <cmd>...]
crq autofix                                  # which repositories crq may fix
crq autofix off REPO --reason "why"          # stop fixing there; watching continues
crq autofix on REPO | crq autofix default REPO
```

It drives every open PR in `CRQ_REPOS` through the same `crq next` oracle and emits one JSON line
per PR per pass (`repo`, `pr`, `action`, `findings`, `dispatched`, `skipped`). Fixing is ON by
default — watching a PR nobody fixes is a queue that reports work and does none. `--no-dispatch`
makes one run an observer, `crq autofix off REPO` stops it for one repository (watching and reviewing
continue there), and having no fix command configured observes with a log line rather than refusing
to start. A PR whose action is `fix` is claimed under compare-and-swap and the
command from `CRQ_DISPATCH_CMD` (or after `--`) runs in a crq-made worktree checked out at that
head, with `CRQ_DISPATCH_REPO`, `CRQ_DISPATCH_PR`, `CRQ_DISPATCH_HEAD` and `CRQ_DISPATCH_FINDINGS`
(a JSON file) in its environment. The command is run directly, not through a shell; quoted
arguments in `CRQ_DISPATCH_CMD` are kept whole. Dispatch is bounded per head by
`CRQ_DISPATCH_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (default 5) and uncapped in parallel unless
`CRQ_DISPATCH_CONCURRENCY` sets a valve — fixing findings spends no account quota, so it does not
queue. While a session holds a PR its round leaves the fire queue (and no second session is started
for that PR, even after its own push supersedes the round): the review would be of a head about to
move. `--once` exits non-zero if any PR or repository could not be checked, so cron cannot mistake a
partial scan for a clean one; a daemon pass logs the failure and carries on to the rest of the fleet.

That dispatch claim is mutually exclusive with the interactive work claim. If an agent has already
called `next`, `wait`, or `loop`, autofix skips the PR. If autofix won first, the interactive caller
receives a conflict or wait action from plain `crq next`; commands that explicitly wait block instead
of editing concurrently. Claim creation fails closed when a recently active autofix host runs an
older binary that does not understand work claims; upgrade that daemon first.

A PR whose head branch lives in a FORK is reviewed like any other but not dispatched: the session
would run an agent over a stranger's code with approvals bypassed and a write token in reach. Set
`CRQ_DISPATCH_FORKS=1` to fix contributor pull requests anyway. That is a trust decision, not a
sandbox — crq has none to offer.
Stop crq reviewing a PR (one write, no window for a daemon to fire in):

```bash
crq hold REPO PR --reason "why"
crq unhold REPO PR
crq hold                      # list
```

A live autoreview daemon that advertises hold support is required when creating a hold.
Creating a hold posts its reason on the pull request. A merged pull request's hold is removed
automatically; a merely closed pull request keeps it in case it is reopened.

With `CRQ_TIDY=1`, crq removes its own spent `@coderabbitai review` / `@codex review` comments as
rounds progress. Automatic tidying is opt-in while older binaries may share the state ref. On demand:

```bash
crq tidy REPO PR [--dry-run]
```

Only comments crq posted (never one it adopted — that comment is someone else's), only while the
comment still reads as that one-line command (an edited one is someone's words), only from rounds
that have progressed, only after the bot answered, only once the comment is too old for crq to adopt
again — older than the head commit, or than a later force-push (a command crq's own retry replaced is
spent regardless, and an unreadable head keeps everything),
and never the bots' own comments. Deletions GitHub refuses are reported in `.failed[]`.

Estimate what a round costs before firing it:

```bash
crq cost REPO PR
```

`.low`/`.high` bound it in US dollars; `.exact` is true only when every reviewer's figure is a real
number; `.unpriced[]` names reviewers crq has no pricing for, so the total is a floor;
`.reviewers[].basis` is the sentence explaining each figure. Only two reviewers can cost anything —
Macroscope bills per KB of diff with a 10 KB minimum (so under ~85 changed lines the $0.50 floor IS
the price and the estimate is exact), and CodeRabbit bills per reviewed file only once the plan
allowance is spent AND usage-based reviews are enabled — and since crq does not yet learn which,
a spent allowance reports the primary as unpriced rather than free. Codex and Cursor Bugbot are covered by their
own subscriptions. The diff basis is the whole head, so this is exact on a PR's first Macroscope
review and an upper bound after that. `.prices_checked_at` is when the published figures were last
verified against the vendors.

Change how fix sessions run, per repository or fleet-wide:

```bash
crq solver REPO                                       # effective settings + where each came from
crq solver set REPO --models opus,sonnet,haiku --effort high --attempts 5
crq solver set REPO --severities minor,potential --ask uncertain
crq solver set REPO --prompt "This project uses bun, never npm."
crq solver set REPO --models gpt-5.6-sol --effort medium --one-pass on --merge squash
crq solver set --fleet --effort medium                # the default every repository inherits
crq solver set REPO --inherit models,effort,severities,ask,forks,skip-authors,one-pass,merge
crq solver clear REPO | crq solver clear --fleet
```

`--one-pass on` is a repository-scoped campaign mode: the first review anywhere on a PR consumes
its only review round, then one isolated fixer/finalizer runs even if the review was clean.
`--merge merge|squash|rebase` requires one-pass and lets the autofix watcher merge only the exact
head that successful session released after GitHub reports it conflict-free. Review and check
status are deliberately ignored because the fixer push makes the one allowed review stale. The
finalizer must integrate the base crq observed, and crq verifies that base immediately before the
merge request. GitHub's merge API atomically guards the head SHA but has no expected-base field, so
a base update racing that final request is included by GitHub's merge transaction. A later push,
failed session, draft, or conflict blocks instead of launching another fixer or merging unverified
code. `crq solver set REPO --inherit one-pass,merge` removes campaign hand-offs while preserving
unrelated repository solver overrides; `crq solver clear REPO` discards every repo solver override.

`--models` is an ordered ranking. A provider/model outage parks that entry until its reported reset
time and immediately tries the next one. These outages do not consume the attempt budget; ordinary
failed fix sessions do, and rotate through the ranking. Exhausting a fix-attempt cycle starts an
increasing cooldown (one hour up to one day), then automatically opens a fresh cycle. If every model
is parked, crq waits for the earliest reset instead of permanently exhausting the PR.

`--severities` limits the findings handed to an unattended agent. `--ask` controls how readily it
stops instead of guessing: only when blocked, when confidence is low, or at the first meaningful
ambiguity. A clarification preserves the attempt and holds the PR with the agent's concrete question.

`--inherit` hands a setting back to the layer beneath. It is required for models, effort, severity
scope, clarification policy, forks, one-pass/merge and
skipped authors because an empty model ranking or effort means "use the agent default", `off` is a
real fork policy, and an empty author list means "skip nobody". `--attempts 0` inherits directly.

Three layers again — env, fleet, repository — with `.sources` naming which answered. The AGENT is
not per repository: it is baked into the session script by `crq autofix install`, because switching
between claude and codex is a different command line rather than a different flag. The selected
model, effort and the extra prompt reach the session through its ENVIRONMENT (`CRQ_FIX_MODEL`, `CRQ_FIX_EFFORT`,
`CRQ_FIX_PROMPT`), since the watcher's argv is fixed when it starts and one watcher handles every
repository — so **reinstall autofix** to pick up a session script that reads them.

Change what every repository inherits:

```bash
crq fleet                                          # effective defaults + where each came from
crq fleet set --min-interval 2m --dry-run          # what it WOULD do; writes nothing
crq fleet set --required coderabbitai,codex        # record it for every host
crq fleet clear                                    # back to this host's env
crq fleet adopt [--dry-run]                        # record THIS host's settings for the fleet
crq fleet env CRQ_SETTLE 120s                      # any single setting, by env name
crq fleet env CRQ_SETTLE --clear
```

`adopt` is for a fleet configured before any of this existed: every answer lives in one machine's
env file, so the dashboard reports "env" beside all of them — true, and useless. It copies only what
CAN be fleet-wide. Identity (`CRQ_REPO`, `CRQ_STATE_REF`, `CRQ_ISSUE`, `CRQ_SCOPE`) and per-host
values (`CRQ_REPOS`, `CRQ_EXCLUDE`, `CRQ_HOST`, `CRQ_WORKSPACE`, `CRQ_DISPATCH_CMD`) are reported as
skipped rather than silently dropped, and a value equal to the built-in default is skipped too —
recording one would pin today's default invisibly. Credentials are never written to state at all.

Three layers, least specific first: this host's env, then the fleet record, then a repository's own
override. `.sources` says per setting which layer the current value came from, so a value reading
`env` is this host's file alone. Always `--dry-run` a reviewer change first: adding a required
reviewer invalidates the "this head was reviewed" marker on every completed round that never had it,
and `.reopened` counts the rounds that would be requeued and reviewed again.

Choose which projects crq reviews at all:

```bash
crq repos                                   # every repository, and where each answer came from
crq repos REPO                              # one repository
crq repos add REPO                          # review it (recorded in shared state)
crq repos remove REPO --reason "<why>"      # stop; --reason is required
crq repos default REPO                      # back to whatever this host's env says
```

`.source` is `state` (a record decided it), `env` (this host's `CRQ_REPOS`), `excluded`
(`CRQ_EXCLUDE`, or the gate repo), `scope` (no allow-list, so all of `CRQ_SCOPE`) or `off`.
`CRQ_EXCLUDE` wins over everything — it is a per-host kill switch. Otherwise a record wins in BOTH
directions, and `.env_conflict` reports a record that turns off a repository a host's `CRQ_REPOS`
still lists. `.lagging_hosts` names hosts whose binary predates enrollment records and still decides
from its own env alone. On a host with no `CRQ_REPOS` at all, a record can only WIDEN what is
scanned: the whole of `CRQ_SCOPE` is still searched owner-wide, and a repository enrolled from
outside that scope is searched by name alongside it.

Choose which bots review one project:

```bash
crq reviewers REPO                                    # effective reviewers + budgets
crq reviewers set REPO --bots codex --required codex  # Codex is the only required co-reviewer
crq reviewers set REPO --no-primary                   # CodeRabbit does not review this project
crq reviewers set REPO --primary                      # ...and back on
crq reviewers clear REPO                              # fleet default again
```

WHICH bot is primary is fleet-wide (its markers are compiled into the classifiers), but whether it
runs on a project is not. `--no-primary` means crq never posts its review command there, never
spends the account quota or the fire slot on it, and never waits for its review — the co-reviewers
resolve those rounds alone. This is the switch for a private repo on a free plan, where the metered
reviewer produces nothing.

`--no-primary` also drops the primary from the effective required set, since a reviewer that does
not run cannot gate. It is refused when nobody else is required, because a round gating on nobody
converges before any bot answers. `lagging_primary_off` in the output names hosts running a binary
that predates the switch: they read the field, write it back untouched, and would still fire the
primary there.

Leaving the primary out of `--required` alone is a weaker thing: it is still asked, and still spends
quota; the round just does not WAIT for it.

`budget: account` means the reviewer is serialized against the shared CodeRabbit allowance;
`budget: none` means it runs immediately. Stored in the shared state ref, so the daemon and agents
cannot disagree. The primary reviewer is fleet-wide.

A finding with no `thread_id` — a review body finding, a review-skipped notice, an outside-diff
remark, an issue-comment finding — has nothing for `resolve` or `decline` to act on, and would otherwise block every future
round on that PR. Judge it, then record the decision:

```bash
crq dismiss REPO PR FINDING_ID [FINDING_ID...] --reason "why this is set aside"
```

`FINDING_ID` is `.findings[].id` — content-derived, not a GitHub node ID, which is why the repo and
PR are required. The dismissal covers the current head only; after a push the next reviewer must
report it again. `crq next` and `crq feedback` report `dismissed: N` so a set-aside finding never
looks lost, and `crq loop` converges on the same filtered list. A finding that HAS a thread is
refused: resolve or decline it instead, so the decision lands where the bot can answer it.

For a SKIPPED review specifically, the two remedies differ: narrowing the PR addresses why the
review was skipped, while `crq dismiss` only records that you chose to proceed at this head.

Current feedback without triggering a review:

```bash
crq feedback OWNER/REPO PR_NUMBER
```

`crq feedback`/`crq loop` also surface still-open findings from earlier commits (unresolved,
non-outdated review threads), so no manual cross-review audit is needed.
Review bodies have no resolution flag: crq retains the latest body before a new round starts, but
suppresses body findings older than the persisted current-head round so addressed feedback is not
re-emitted. Unresolved cross-commit threads remain visible.

Long waits are not hangs. Queue and reviewer progress stays on the CLI's stderr; GitHub rate-limit
and outage recovery lives in the `crq serve` log. Stdout stays reserved for the final JSON.

Keeping a loop alive is not your problem. `crq next` returns immediately, and `crq wait` owns no
review round, so neither leaves queue state for a harness to orphan. Their work claim is deliberately
temporary. If either is killed, run it again and the answer comes from persisted state. Never
substitute a `crq status` polling loop, a `gh api` poll, a timer, or a guessed review latency for
`crq wait`.

Agent communication rule: do not relay every stderr progress line or send repeated "still waiting"
updates. Report a real state change — fired, findings, `push`, convergence, timeout, a
rate-limit/window change, a network outage or recovery — or answer when the user asks. If the only
new information is elapsed time on the same wait, stay quiet.

Fleet review:

```bash
crq autoreview
```

Run exactly one long-lived autoreview daemon. Manual `crq loop` calls and autoreview share the same
idempotent queue entry, so after a push either one may enqueue first and the other only re-attaches.
Never start a second watcher or post a direct CodeRabbit trigger to "help" the daemon.

Autoreview skips PRs authored by dependabot by default (`CRQ_AUTOREVIEW_SKIP_AUTHORS`,
comma-separated logins; set empty to include bot PRs). The autofix watcher honours the same list —
it drives PRs through the mutating `crq next`, so a skipped author is neither reviewed nor fixed.
Manual `crq review` ignores this filter.
For an intentionally low-risk PR that already had enough local review, include the hidden
`<!-- crq:skip-autoreview -->` marker in its body before creation. Fleet autoreview skips it, while
an explicit `crq loop` still works. Configure or disable the exact marker with
`CRQ_AUTOREVIEW_SKIP_MARKER`.

Diagnostics only:

```bash
crq doctor
crq status
crq debug state
crq debug refresh
```

JSON contract: `findings` is always an array. Each finding always has `bot`,
`severity`, `title`, `body`, and `source`. The location fields `path`, `line`,
`url`, and `thread_id` are optional and omitted when CodeRabbit doesn't supply
them (e.g. review-body / outside-diff findings have no `path`/`line`, and only
inline review threads carry a `thread_id`) — parse them defensively.

Optional local preflight: if CodeRabbit CLI is installed, `crq preflight --type uncommitted`
can review local git changes before pushing and normalize the JSON stream. Exit 2 means "come back
later" — either a timeout or `status: "rate_limited"`, with `.retry_after` and `.error_type`. That
block is the SAME account quota PR reviews spend, so crq records it for the fleet and `.quota` says
whether it did. When shared state already records a live account block, preflight exits 0 without
calling the CLI and reports `status: "skipped"`, `.skip_reason`, and `.blocked_until`; an unreadable
state falls back to the normal local review. `CRQ_PREFLIGHT_SKIP_BLOCKED` controls this behavior and
defaults to `1`; set it to `0` to force the CLI request. That does not replace
`crq loop`; only `crq loop` queues and waits for GitHub PR review feedback.
